Parents brought children who knew Jackson through videos and family playlists, while older fans recalled watching him perform as the dazzling young lead singer of the Jackson 5.

“I remember seeing that little boy with the big voice,” said one woman who said she had followed Jackson’s career for decades. “You knew right away he was special. Nobody moved like him. Nobody sang like him.”

For younger admirers, Jackson’s legacy was tied to music videos, choreography and the era-defining success of albums such as “Off the Wall,” “Thriller” and “Bad.” Fans described learning his dance steps from television, copying his glove and hat, and seeing him as an artist who set the standard for pop performance.

“He made you want to dance even when you were sad,” another fan said. “That’s why we’re here. We’re sad, but we’re also celebrating what he gave us.”

Jackson’s connection to the Apollo carried particular resonance. The theater, opened in the early 20th century and later known worldwide for its Amateur Night, became a symbol of Harlem’s cultural power and a proving ground for Black performers during decades when mainstream entertainment venues were often segregated or exclusionary. To stand beneath its marquee in mourning, many fans said, was to place Jackson within a broader history of African American music and achievement.

Although Jackson’s later life was marked by controversy, health concerns and intense public scrutiny, those gathered in Harlem focused largely on his musical legacy and the emotional bond they felt with him. They spoke of the joy of his songs, the innovation of his videos, and the sense that a performer who had been famous for nearly his entire life had somehow remained personal to millions.

As evening approached, the memorial continued to grow. Candles flickered near the curb. Fans signed banners and left messages that read “Rest in Peace, Michael,” “King of Pop Forever” and “Thank You for the Music.” Some stood for hours, reluctant to leave.

“He gave his whole life to entertaining people,” one mourner said. “The least we can do is come here and say thank you.”

CNN’s Aspen Steib contributed to this report.
